adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

kurals.tamil:
அணங்குகொல் ஆய்மயில் கொல்லோ கனங்குழை
மாதர்கொல் மாலும்என் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anangukol aaimayil kollo kananguzhai
maatharkol maalumen nenju.
kurals.meaning: Is she a goddess, a rare peacock, or a human girl wearing heavy earrings? My heart is bewildered and cannot tell.
kurals.elementary: Imagine seeing a sunset so beautiful that you stop and wonder whether it is real or a painting. The young man in this verse sees a girl for the first time and is so amazed that he cannot decide whether she is a goddess, a lovely peacock, or an ordinary girl.
kurals.university: This kural opens the Kamattuppal and its Kalaviyal (the section on premarital, 'secret' love), voicing the hero's (talaivan's) first sight of the heroine. The chapter title combines takai (தகை, 'beauty, grace'), anangu (அணங்கு, a goddess or spirit that afflicts those who approach it) and uruttal (உறுத்தல், 'causing'), so it means the distress her beauty inflicts. The three-way doubt, anangu-kol, aaimayil-kollo, maathar-kol (goddess? choice peahen? woman?), is a classical Tamil figure of bewilderment (aiyam), and maalum (மாலும், 'is confused, infatuated') names the state. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses kananguzhai as 'a woman wearing heavy ear-ornaments', the detail that hints she is human after all; Pope renders 'Goddess? or peafowl rare?... All wildered is my mind!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And neither among celestials, nor among Yakshas, nor among men was anybody possessed of such beauty, seen or heard of before.”
hinduism.explanation: The Nala episode of the Mahabharata describes Damayanti as a beauty that no god, spirit or human could match.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's hero, the narrator can place her beauty neither among gods nor among humans.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 53 (Nalopakhyana; tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the same 'celestial or human?' frame, though told by a narrator rather than a bewildered lover.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?”
christianity.explanation: In the Song of Songs onlookers ask who this woman can be, comparing her to dawn, moon and sun.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts react to beauty with a startled question about who, or what, she really is.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); strong match on wondering 'who is she?', though without the explicit goddess/human doubt.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, ‘Perfect is Allāh! This is not a man; this is none but a noble angel.’”
islam.explanation: When the women of Egypt first see Joseph, they are so struck that they cut their hands and declare he cannot be human.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a first sight of beauty makes the viewers doubt whether the person is human or heavenly.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (footnote markers removed); near one-to-one on the 'not human but angelic' reaction, with genders reversed.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud lists four women of the Bible who were of outstanding beauty: Sarah, Rahab, Abigail and Esther, and records rabbinic remarks on how powerfully their beauty affected those who saw or even named them.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis treat extraordinary beauty as a real force that can unsettle the mind of an onlooker.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's bewildered hero is an example of exactly that unsettling force.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the passage, not checked against a live text this session; thematic only, with no goddess-or-human doubt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What do you think, Nanda? Which is lovelier, better looking, more charming: the Sakyan girl, the envy of the countryside, or these 500 dove-footed nymphs?”
buddhism.explanation: To cure Nanda's longing for a beautiful girl, the Buddha takes him to heaven and asks him to compare her with celestial nymphs.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's hero cannot tell a girl from a goddess; the Buddha deliberately sets a girl beside goddesses to loosen that spell.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it shares the human-versus-celestial comparison but uses it to teach detachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though those who possess the three Guptis, cannot be disturbed even by well-adorned goddesses, still it is recommended to monks to live by themselves, as this is wholesome in every way.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that a monk whose mind, speech and body are fully guarded (the three guptis) cannot be shaken even by adorned goddesses, but still advises seclusion.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows the opposite case: an unguarded heart is thrown into confusion by a beauty that seems divine.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares the goddess-like beauty and the disturbed mind, but from the renunciant's side and as a contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I implore your aid- but tell me, are you a goddess or are you a mortal woman?”
greek_mythology.explanation: Shipwrecked Odysseus, meeting the princess Nausicaa on the shore, cannot tell whether she is the goddess Artemis or a human girl.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact question, goddess or human maiden, asked at a first meeting.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu (Butler's hyphen kept); a near one-to-one parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...is amazed when he sees any one having a godlike face or form, which is the expression of divine beauty; and at first a shudder runs through him, and again the old awe steals over him.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates describes the soul that sees earthly beauty and is reminded of divine beauty, so that it shudders and feels awe before the beloved as before a god.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato explains philosophically why the Kural's hero confuses a girl with a goddess.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; strong match on beauty seeming divine and stunning the viewer.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

kurals.tamil:
நோக்கினாள் நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல் தாக்கணங்கு
தானைக்கொண் டன்ன துடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Nokkinaal nokkethir nokkuthal thaakkanangu
thaanaikkon tanna thudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: When she returns my look, her answering glance is like an attacking goddess who has brought a whole army with her.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been looked at so seriously that you suddenly felt shy and could not look back? Here the young man looks at the girl, and when she looks back at him he feels as if an entire army has charged at him.
kurals.university: The kural turns on the repeated root nokku (நோக்கு, 'look'): nokkinaal ('she who looked'), nokkethir ('against my look') and nokkuthal ('the looking back'). Thaakkanangu (தாக்கணங்கு) is an anangu that strikes or attacks on its own, and thaanai (தானை) is an army; Mu. Varadarasanar explains that her return glance is like such a self-attacking deity arriving with a whole army. Commentators in the Parimelazhagar line take the point to be that one glance already wounds, so a returned glance doubles the assault. Pope renders: 'As if the matchless goddess' hand / Led forth an armed band.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava, Kama, the god of love, waits with his flower-bow as Parvati approaches the meditating Shiva, and shoots at the moment her glance meets his, so that even the great ascetic is shaken.
hinduism.explanation: Love in Indian poetry is pictured as an archer-god whose arrows fly with a beloved's glance.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise turns a returned glance into an armed attack by a deity.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a live text; strong thematic fit on a glance as a divine weapon.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs finds the beloved both beautiful and overwhelming, like an army with banners.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural uses the same military image: her look arrives like an army.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); the beauty-as-army image is a close match.

islam.quote_or_event: “And women in the city said, ‘The wife of al-ʿAzeez is seeking to seduce her slave boy; he has impassioned her with love. Indeed, we see her [to be] in clear error.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the wife of al-Aziz as having been overpowered by love for Joseph through his beauty.
islam.tie_back: Both texts show beauty overpowering the one who looks at it, though the Qur'an judges the passion as error.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; only a partial fit, since it contains no image of a returned glance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You have captured my heart, / My own, my bride, / You have captured my heart / With one [glance] of your eyes, / With one coil of your necklace.”
judaism.explanation: The lover says that a single glance of the beloved's eyes has taken his heart captive.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, says one returned look is enough to overcome him.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 4:9 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (line breaks marked with slashes); near one-to-one on a glance conquering the heart.

buddhism.explanation: In the Padhana Sutta the Buddha-to-be names the forces Mara sends against him as armies, and sensual passion leads them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's image of a glance arriving like an army matches the Buddhist picture of desire as an attacking army.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 3.2, Padhana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the army image matches closely, but the Buddhist text resists the attack instead of celebrating it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Śramaṇa, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's discipline lists glances among the things a monk must not dwell on, because they disturb the mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows why: a single returned glance overwhelms the one who meets it.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's italic transliteration written here as Śramaṇa); it agrees that a glance is powerful but answers it with renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's tale, Cupid shoots Apollo with a golden arrow so that the god falls in love the instant he sees the nymph Daphne, and even the mighty archer-god is helpless.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek and Roman myth make love an armed god whose arrows strike through the eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's 'attacking goddess with an army' is the Tamil form of love as a weapon-bearing deity.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, not checked against a live text; strong on love as an attack, less on the returned glance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...as he receives the effluence of beauty through the eyes, the wing moistens and he warms.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes beauty as a stream that enters the lover through the eyes and overpowers him.
philosophy.tie_back: For the Kural, too, the eyes are the gate through which the attack comes.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; good on beauty entering through sight, though without the military image.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

kurals.tamil:
பண்டறியேன் கூற்றென் பதனை இனியறிந்தேன்
பெண்டகையால் பேரமர்க் கட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pandariyen kootren pathanai iniyarinthen
pendakaiyaal peramark kattu.
kurals.meaning: I never knew before what they call Death; now I know it: it has a woman's grace and large eyes that make war.
kurals.elementary: People sometimes say a scary film 'nearly killed' them, even though they were safe. The young man jokes in the same way: he had only heard of Death in stories, but now he has met it, in the shape of a girl with big, powerful eyes.
kurals.university: Kootru (கூற்று) is Death personified, Yama, the 'one who divides' body from life. Pandariyen ('I did not know before') and iniyarinthen ('now I have learned') frame a mock discovery. The second line packs pen-takai (பெண்டகை, 'womanly grace') with per-amar-kan (பேரமர்க்கண், 'large eyes that do battle'); Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as 'it has a woman's nature and large eyes that make war', while Kalaignar speaks of eye-arrows. The commentarial tradition treats the hyperbole as the lover's helplessness, not a moral judgment on the woman. Pope: 'Death's form I formerly / Knew not; but now 'tis plain to me; / He comes in lovely maiden's guise.' Identical on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material modes of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring, sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls kama, desire, the all-devouring enemy of the world.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural playfully treats the beloved's eyes as Death; the Gita seriously treats desire itself as a devouring enemy.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; it shares desire as a destroyer, but the Gita's tone is moral warning, not romantic hyperbole.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that a woman's eyes can capture a man and lead him to ruin.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes the eyes the weapon that takes a man's life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); strong on deadly eyes, but Proverbs is warning against an adulteress, unlike the Kural's innocent heroine.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and [thus] be of the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: Joseph asks God to protect him, knowing how strongly beauty and attraction can pull even a righteous man.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat the pull of beauty as a danger strong enough to overcome a person.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a next-best match on beauty's dangerous power, without the Death image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is fierce as death, / Passion is mighty as Sheol; / Its darts are darts of fire, / A blazing flame.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs compares love to death and the grave and speaks of its fiery darts.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, puts love and Death side by side and gives love weapons.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 8:6 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; a close match on love as death-like and armed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is like froth, penetrating its mirage-like nature, and plucking out Mara's flower-tipped arrows of sensuality, go beyond sight of the King of Death!”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada links Mara's flower-arrows of desire with the realm of the King of Death.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural discovers that the eyes of desire are Death itself; the Dhammapada makes the same link and urges escape.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a strong match on love-arrows and Death, used as a warning.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares pleasures to a lovely fruit that turns out to be deadly poison.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural finds that something beautiful can be Death in disguise, which is the same idea.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong on beauty that kills, but used as a renunciant warning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Small wonder that Trojans and Achaeans should endure so much and so long, for the sake of a woman so marvellously and divinely lovely.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The Trojan elders, watching Helen, admit that her beauty explains a war that has brought death to so many.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the elders tie a woman's beauty directly to death and battle.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; beauty and death are linked, though through war rather than through the lover's own heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus says that the sight of true beauty brings wonder and a delicious trouble, longing and love, and a trembling that is all delight.
philosophy.explanation: For Plotinus, beauty strikes the soul with an overwhelming and pleasurable shock.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural expresses the same overwhelming shock in the playful language of meeting Death.
philosophy.source: Plotinus, Enneads I.6.4 (tr. Stephen MacKenna; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of MacKenna's wording, not checked against a live text; it fits beauty's shock but has no Death image.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

kurals.tamil:
கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றத்தால் பெண்டகைப்
பேதைக்கு அமர்த்தன கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kandaar uyirunnum thottraththaal pendakaip
pethaikku amarththana kan.
kurals.meaning: This gentle, innocent girl has eyes that seem to drink the life of anyone who sees them, so her eyes are at odds with her soft nature.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kitten with huge, shining eyes: it is small and gentle, yet one look can make everyone in the room stop what they are doing. The young man sees that the girl is shy and gentle, but her eyes are so powerful that they seem to belong to someone much fiercer.
kurals.university: Uyir-unnum (உயிருண்ணும்) means 'devouring life', and kandaar (கண்டார்) 'those who see', so her eyes have a look that eats the life of every viewer. Pethai (பேதை) here means an innocent young girl, not a 'fool', and pen-takai (பெண்டகை) is womanly grace. The key verb amarththana (அமர்த்தன) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'were at variance with one another', i.e. the eyes contradict her gentle nature; Solomon Pappaiah adds that they 'war against' her character and understanding. Pope renders: 'In sweet simplicity, / A woman's gracious form hath she; / But yet those eyes, that drink my life, / Are with the form at strife!' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And as he gazed on that lady of sweet smiles. Nala's love increased, but desirous of keeping his truth, he suppressed his passion.”
hinduism.explanation: When Nala sees Damayanti, her sweet beauty stirs a powerful love that he must struggle to master.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a gentle, smiling beauty has an overwhelming effect on the one who looks.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 55 (Nalopakhyana; tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (the full stop before 'Nala's' is as printed); it shares gentle beauty's power, not the contrast between eyes and nature.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.”
christianity.explanation: The lover says one look from the beloved's eyes has carried his heart away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same claim: her eyes take the viewer's very life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); strong on overpowering eyes, without the contrast to her gentle nature.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells believers to lower their gaze, recognising how much power the eyes have over the heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural describes the force of a look; the Qur'an answers that force with restraint of the gaze.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API (quoted up to 'purer for them'); it is a response to the gaze's power, not a description of it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Turn your eyes away from me, / For they overwhelm me!”
judaism.explanation: The lover begs the beloved to look away because her eyes overpower him.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's eyes that 'drink life' are the same overwhelming eyes.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 6:5 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; near one-to-one on overpowering eyes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The Destroyer brings under his sway the person of distracted mind who, insatiate in sense desires, only plucks the flowers (of pleasure).”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that the Destroyer (death) takes control of the person carried away by sense desire.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's 'life-devouring' eyes describe that same capture from inside the lover's experience.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a reasonable but partial fit, framed as moral warning.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of 'colours,' will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's teaching says that passion for what the eye sees destroys a person the way a flame draws a moth to its death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's eyes that 'drink the life' of the viewer are the flame, and the lover is the moth.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com ('colour' is Jacobi's term for all visible form); strong on sight that kills, used as a warning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's version, Medusa was once a beautiful maiden; after her transformation her gaze turned everyone who looked at her to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes a woman's eyes literally deadly to anyone who meets them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's 'life-devouring' eyes are a playful version of the deadly gaze, set against the girl's gentleness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; the deadly gaze matches, but Medusa is monstrous and the Kural's girl is not.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's Symposium, Diotima describes Eros as a paradox: poor and soft in one way, yet a bold and mighty hunter who is always weaving snares.
philosophy.explanation: Plato sees love as made of opposites, gentle and fierce at once.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural finds the same opposition in the girl, whose gentle nature contrasts with her conquering eyes.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; the gentle-and-fierce paradox matches only loosely.

adhikaram.english: Mental Disturbance Caused by Her Beauty

kurals.tamil:
கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ மடவரல்
நோக்கமிம் மூன்றும் உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kootramo kanno pinaiyo madavaral
nokkamim moondrum udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: Is it Death, is it an eye, or is it a shy doe? This young girl's look has all three natures at once.
kurals.elementary: Some things can be several things at once: a rainbow is pretty, a bit mysterious and gone in a moment. The young man finds the girl's look like that. It is powerful enough to knock him over, warm like a friendly eye, and shy like a little deer.
kurals.university: The question again uses the doubting particle -o: kootramo (கூற்றமோ, 'Death?'), kanno (கண்ணோ, 'an eye?'), pinaiyo (பிணையோ, 'a hind/doe?'). Madavaral (மடவரல்) is a young, innocent woman, and nokkam (நோக்கம்) her look. Commentators explain the three qualities differently: Mu. Varadarasanar simply lists Death, eye and doe; Solomon Pappaiah reads the eye as a glance that spreads all over the viewer's body and the doe as a timid, fearful look; Puliyur Kesikan has 'the afflicting Death, the darting eye, the startled doe'. The point is that one look combines danger, warmth and shyness. Pope: 'Is it death's dart? or eye's bright beams? / Or fawn's shy glance? All three appear.' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa's Shakuntala begins with King Dushyanta chasing a frightened deer into a hermitage, where he meets Shakuntala, a girl raised among fawns, whose shy, darting glances the play repeatedly compares to a deer's.
hinduism.explanation: Sanskrit love poetry often likens a young woman's timid glance to a fawn's.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's pinai (doe) uses the same image of a shy, deer-like look that overwhelms the hero.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play's well-known deer motif, not checked against a live text; it matches the doe-glance but not the Death element.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs repeatedly ties love to gentle deer, roes and hinds.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's look has the shyness of a doe, the same animal the Song uses for love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); only the deer image matches, with no three-fold look.

islam.quote_or_event: “And [for them are] fair women with large, [beautiful] eyes,”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the companions of Paradise by their large, beautiful eyes, which commentators often compare to the eyes of a gazelle.
islam.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes a woman's large, deer-like eyes the centre of her beauty.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the gazelle comparison belongs to the commentaries, not the verse, so the match is partial.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs urges a man to delight in the wife of his youth and likens her to a loving doe and a graceful mountain goat.
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew Bible, like Tamil poetry, uses the doe as an image of a beloved woman's grace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's pinai, the shy doe in the girl's look, is the same figure.
judaism.source: Proverbs 5:18-19 (paraphrase; cf. JPS Tanakh on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; shares only the doe image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When Mara fails to break the newly awakened Buddha, his three daughters, Craving, Discontent and Passion, try in many forms to tempt him, and fail.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist texts picture desire as several alluring forms working together.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's look holds three natures at once; Mara sends three daughters, each a face of desire.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; a next-best match on a threefold allure, with no doe or eye imagery.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an impassioned deer allured (by a song) rushes into death, without being satisfied with the sound.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the deer, drawn helplessly by music, as an example of how passion for a sense object leads to death.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural brings together a deer and Death in one look; Jain teaching joins the same two images.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, as given in his summary of vv. 35-47)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; deer and death are both present, but here the deer is the victim rather than the beloved's look.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The hunter Actaeon happens to see the goddess Artemis bathing; she turns him into a stag, and he is killed by his own hounds.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this myth a single sight of divine beauty brings a deer's form and death together.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's look combines Death and a deer in the same way, though gently and playfully.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; it shares sight, deer and death, but the myth is a punishment tale.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Edmund Burke separated the beautiful (small, smooth, delicate, inspiring love) from the sublime (vast, powerful, inspiring a kind of terror), while noting that strong experiences can mix the two.
philosophy.explanation: Burke's aesthetics explains how one sight can feel both gentle and terrifying.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's look is both a gentle doe (the beautiful) and Death (the terrible) at once.
philosophy.source: Edmund Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757), Parts 2-3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Burke's well-known distinction, not checked against a live text; an analytical rather than poetic parallel.

kurals.tamil:
கொடும்புருவம் கோடா மறைப்பின் நடுங்கஞர்
செய்யல மன்இவள் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kodumpuruvam kodaa maraippin nadungagnar
seyyala manival kan.
kurals.meaning: If her curved eyebrows would only stay straight and screen her eyes, her eyes would not cause me this trembling distress.
kurals.elementary: When the sun is too bright, a cap with a peak shades your eyes so you are not dazzled. The young man wishes her eyebrows would act like that cap and shade her eyes, so her look would not make him so nervous.
kurals.university: Kodum-puruvam (கொடும்புருவம்) means the 'curved' or 'cruel' brows; kodum carries both senses, so the curve itself is accused. Kodaa (கோடா, 'without bending') and maraippin (மறைப்பின், 'if they hid') give the wish: if the brows stayed straight and screened the eyes. Nadung-agnar (நடுங்கஞர்) is 'trembling distress', and man (மன்) adds regret, 'surely they would not...'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both read it as 'if the bent brows stood straight and hid them, her eyes would not cause me trembling sorrow'. The image draws on the Indian convention of brows as a drawn bow from which the eyes shoot. Pope: 'If cruel eye-brow's bow, / Unbent, would veil those glances now.' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad compares the body to a chariot, the senses to horses and the mind to the reins: only a person who keeps the reins firm stops the senses from running wild.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu teaching treats control over what reaches us through the senses as the key to a steady mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural wishes for a 'rein' on the eyes, the brows acting as a screen that would spare him distress.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; a next-best match on restraining sight, with no eyebrow image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me: thy hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Gilead.”
christianity.explanation: The lover asks the beloved to turn her eyes away because they overpower him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same wish: if only her eyes were screened, he would stop trembling.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); a near one-to-one wish that the overpowering eyes be turned away.

islam.quote_or_event: “And she certainly determined [to seduce] him, and he would have inclined to her had he not seen the proof [i.e., sign] of his Lord.”
islam.explanation: Joseph is kept from yielding only because a sign from God came between him and temptation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural wishes for a screen between him and her eyes; Joseph is saved by a divine screen.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API (quoted to 'his Lord'); a next-best match on a protecting barrier.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Your eyes are like doves / Behind your veil.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs praises the beloved's eyes as they appear softened behind a veil.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural wishes her eyes were veiled by her brows, so their power would be softened.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 4:1 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; strong on screened eyes, though the Song finds them lovely rather than dangerous.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Visuddhimagga tells of the elder Mahatissa, who passed a woman laughing on the road and, guarding his senses, noticed only her teeth, which became for him an object of meditation on the body.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist sense restraint means not letting the eye seize on beauty, so it cannot disturb the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural wishes for a screen over her eyes; the monk builds that screen inside his own mind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story, not checked against a live text; it fits guarding the eyes, though from the opposite side.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not to look at, nor to long for, not to think of, nor to praise, womankind: this is becoming the meditation of the noble ones, and it is always wholesome to those who delight in chastity.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana makes not looking the first step of a monk's chastity.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover wishes the sight could be screened off; Jain discipline screens it by choice.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares the 'block the sight' idea, framed as renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...from whose eyes as they glanced flowed love that unnerves the limbs: and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that love flows from the Graces' eyes and singles out their glance beneath their brows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, places the danger in the eyes beneath curved brows.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; a close match on limb-loosening glances under the brows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal remarked that if Cleopatra's nose had been shorter, the whole face of the earth would have changed.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal's point is that a tiny feature of a face can decide enormous outcomes.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes everything depend on one small feature, the curve of her eyebrows.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line, not checked against a live text; a witty structural parallel rather than a shared teaching.

kurals.tamil:
கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம் மாதர்
படாஅ முலைமேல் துகில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadaaak kalitrinmer katpadaam maathar
padaaa mulaimel thukil.
kurals.meaning: The garment draped over the maiden's bosom is like the cloth placed over the eyes of a raging elephant: a covering that keeps a dangerous power in check.
kurals.elementary: At festivals, big temple elephants sometimes wear a decorated cloth over their faces. It looks beautiful, but it also helps keep the elephant calm. The young man thinks the scarf the girl wears works the same way, both lovely and protective.
kurals.university: Kadaaak kalitru (கடாஅக் களிறு) is a bull elephant in must (mada), and katpadaam (கட்படாம்) the cloth hung over its face and eyes to keep it from charging. Thukil (துகில்) is fine cloth worn by the maathar (மாதர், young woman). The lengthened forms kadaaa and padaaa are alapedai, vowel extension for metre. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read the comparison as protective: the covering stops her beauty from 'killing' the onlooker, just as the face-cloth restrains the elephant. Pope: 'As veil o'er angry eyes / Of raging elephant that lies, / The silken cincture's folds invest / This maiden's panting breast.' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavad Gita says that a person of steady wisdom draws the senses back from their objects as a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell.
hinduism.explanation: Restraint is pictured as a protective covering that keeps the senses from being dragged away.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's cloth is also a protective covering that keeps a dangerous force in check.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked this session; a next-best match on covering as restraint.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;”
christianity.explanation: Paul's letter recommends modest clothing over showy adornment.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, sees the covering garment as a modest restraint on beauty's power.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); shares modest covering, not the elephant image.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and to wrap [a portion of] their headcovers over their chests and not expose their adornment...”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an asks believing women to draw their head-coverings over their chests as a sign of modesty.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's image is of exactly such a covering cloth, which it treats as a restraint on beauty's force.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on the quran.com API (excerpt marked with ellipses); a close match on the covering itself, though the purpose is religious modesty.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Rebekah first sees Isaac coming toward her across the field, she takes her veil and covers herself.
judaism.explanation: In Genesis, covering oneself at a first meeting is a sign of modesty and dignity.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's covering cloth likewise marks modesty and calms the power of first sight.
judaism.source: Genesis 24:64-65 (paraphrase; cf. JPS Tanakh on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; it shares the protective covering at a first meeting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Formerly this mind wandered about as it liked, where it wished and according to its pleasure, but now I shall thoroughly master it with wisdom as a mahout controls with his ankus an elephant in rut.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures the untrained mind as an elephant in rut that must be kept in check.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same raging elephant and the means of restraining it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; same elephant-in-rut image, applied to the mind rather than to beauty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Aphrodite lends Hera her embroidered band, in which love, desire and persuasive charm are woven, and its power overcomes even Zeus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you see an attractive person, you will find that self-restraint is the ability you have against your desire.”

kurals.tamil:
ஒண்ணுதற் கோஒ உடைந்ததே ஞாட்பினுள்
நண்ணாரும் உட்குமென் பீடு.
kurals.transliteration:
Onnuthar koo udainthathe gnaatpinul
nannaarum utkumen peedu.
kurals.meaning: Alas! My might, which made even my enemies tremble on the battlefield, has broken before her bright forehead alone.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a champion wrestler who has never lost, but who becomes shy and tongue-tied when he meets someone he really admires. The young man is a brave warrior, yet one look at the girl's shining face makes all his toughness melt away.
kurals.university: On-nuthal (ஒண்ணுதல்) is a 'bright forehead', a standard metonymy for the heroine. Koo (கோஒ) is an exclamation of dismay lengthened by alapedai. Gnaatpu (ஞாட்பு) is the battlefield, nannaar (நண்ணார்) foes (literally 'those who do not draw near', i.e. are not friends), utkum (உட்கும்) 'fear', and peedu (பீடு) 'valour, prowess'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads: 'my strength, which made even foes fear in battle, has been defeated by her bright forehead'; Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take nannaar as including those who only heard of his fame. The hero (talaivan) of Tamil akam poetry is ideally a warrior, so the defeat is sharpened. Pope: 'my might, / That awed my foemen in the fight, / By lustre of that beaming brow / Borne down, lies broken now!' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As a boat on the water is swept away by a strong wind, even one of the senses on which the mind focuses can carry away a man's intelligence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a single sense the mind fixes on can overpower even a strong person.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior is carried away in exactly this way by a single sight.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.67 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; a strong fit on one sense overpowering a strong mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him.”
christianity.explanation: Samson, the mightiest warrior of Israel, loses his strength through his love for Delilah.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's hero, a famous warrior's strength is broken through love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); strong on a hero undone by love, though Delilah's betrayal has no parallel in the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “She said, ‘That is the one about whom you blamed me. And I certainly sought to seduce him, but he firmly refused...’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents Joseph as the one whose strength of will did not break before attraction.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows a strong man's will breaking; Joseph is the Qur'an's contrasting model of firmness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API (excerpt); a contrast rather than a parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city.’”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah defines real strength as mastering one's own desires, not defeating enemies.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior beats his foes but cannot master his heart, which is exactly Ben Zoma's point.

judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (excerpt); a strong conceptual match between outward and inward strength.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a storm throws down a weak tree, so does Mara overpower the man who lives for the pursuit of pleasures, who is uncontrolled in his senses...”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the person whose senses are uncontrolled is knocked down by Mara like a tree in a storm.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's warrior, strong in battle but unguarded in sense, is knocked down in the same way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; good on a strength overthrown through the senses.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi's strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion.”
jainism.explanation: The prince and monk Rathanemi sees Rajimati unexpectedly and his strength of will breaks, until she brings him back to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's 'my might is broken' is told from the inside; the Uttaradhyayana describes the same collapse from outside.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's italic g written here as plain g); a close match on a strong man's will broken by beauty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod makes Eros the power that defeats the strength and judgment of gods and men alike.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's warrior, whose valour breaks at one sight, is one of Eros's victims.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius opens his poem with Mars, the lord of war, lying in the lap of Venus, defeated by the eternal wound of love and gazing up at her.

kurals.tamil:
பிணையேர் மடநோக்கும் நாணும் உடையாட்கு
அணியெவனோ ஏதில தந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Pinaiyer madanokkum naanum udaiyaatku
aniyevano ethila thanthu.
kurals.meaning: She already has the gentle, doe-like look and natural modesty; what use are other ornaments, which have nothing to do with her, on such a girl?
kurals.elementary: A flower in a garden is already beautiful; you do not need to paint it or stick glitter on it. The young man feels the same about the girl: her kind eyes and shyness are her real jewels, so ordinary jewellery adds nothing.
kurals.university: Pinai-er (பிணையேர்) means 'like a doe', mada-nokku (மடநோக்கு) 'an innocent, gentle look', and naanum (நாணும்) 'and modesty'. Naanam (நாணம்) is one of the classical feminine virtues in Tamil poetics, alongside madam (innocence), accham (fear) and payirppu (delicacy). Ethila (ஏதில) is 'alien, unrelated', so other ornaments are foreign to her true beauty. Mu. Varadarasanar asks why one should put unrelated jewels on her; Kalaignar contrasts natural (iyarkai) and artificial (seyarkai) ornaments. Pope: 'Like tender fawn's her eye; / Clothed on is she with modesty; / What added beauty can be lent / By alien ornament?' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Act I of Kalidasa's Shakuntala, King Dushyanta notices that Shakuntala's rough bark garment does not dim her beauty, and reflects that a lovely form is adorned by anything, as a lotus stays lovely though covered with moss.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa makes the point that true beauty needs no costly ornament.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question: what can outside ornaments add to natural grace?
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not checked against a live text; a near one-to-one idea.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that a gentle, quiet spirit is the true ornament, worth more than gold or fine clothes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, names gentleness and modesty as her real ornaments.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); a near one-to-one match.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, We have bestowed upon you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks the inner 'clothing' of righteousness above every outward garment and adornment.
islam.tie_back: The Kural ranks inner modesty above outward jewels in the same way.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API (quoted to 'that is best'); a strong match on inner over outer adornment.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Grace is deceptive, / Beauty is illusory; / It is for her fear of GOD / That a woman is to be praised.”
judaism.explanation: The poem of the 'woman of valour' places a woman's worth in her character rather than in outward charm.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, values her inner qualities over anything added from outside.
judaism.source: Proverbs 31:30 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (small-caps GOD written in capitals); a good match on character over appearance, though Proverbs discounts even natural beauty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Of all the fragrances — sandal, tagara, blue lotus and jasmine — the fragrance of virtue is the sweetest.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ranks virtue above every costly perfume.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ranks modesty above costly ornaments in the same spirit.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; same inner-over-outer ranking, applied to perfume instead of jewels.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue...”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, praised earlier as beautiful, is finally honoured for her self-control and virtue.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural, too, makes modesty and virtue a woman's chief adornment.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; excerpt)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (excerpt); a reasonable match on virtue as a woman's glory, without the ornament contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod, the gods adorn the first woman, Pandora, with golden necklaces, a crown of flowers and fine clothing, yet her outward splendour hides the trouble she brings.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth sets dazzling outward adornment against what lies within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural reverses Pandora: her inner qualities are the real beauty and outward ornaments add nothing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; a contrast rather than a parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “We should, therefore, fix our attention on making them sensible that they are valued for the appearance of decent, modest and discreet behavior.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus objects that young women are taught to rely on adornment, and says they should know they are valued for modesty and good conduct.

philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 40 (tr. Elizabeth Carter, as revised on classics.mit.edu)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong match on modesty over adornment.

kurals.tamil:
உண்டார்கண் அல்லது அடுநறாக் காமம்போல்
கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Undaarkan allathu adunaraak kaamampol
kandaar makizhseydhal indru.
kurals.meaning: Strong drink delights only those who drink it; it cannot, as love does, delight people who merely look.
kurals.elementary: A treat only makes you happy once you eat it. But seeing someone you love, like a parent coming home, makes you happy just by looking. The young man says love is special in this way: just seeing her fills him with joy.
kurals.university: Undaar (உண்டார்) is 'those who have drunk' and kandaar (கண்டார்) 'those who have seen'; the pairing undaar / kandaar carries the whole comparison. Adu-nara (அடுநறா) is literally 'cooked (boiled, distilled) toddy', i.e. strong drink, and makizh-seythal (மகிழ்செய்தல்) is 'causing delight or intoxication'. Mu. Varadarasanar: toddy intoxicates only those who drink it, not, like kaamam, those who merely see it. The verse closes the chapter by turning the hero's distress into joy, and its praise of love over drink sits easily with the Kural's earlier chapter against intoxicants (Kallunnaamai, ch. 93). Pope: 'The palm-tree's fragrant wine, / To those who taste yields joys divine; / But love hath rare felicity / For those that only see!' Identical on both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita traces how merely dwelling on what the senses present gives rise to attachment and desire.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates the fact that mere seeing intoxicates; the Gita analyses the same process as a danger.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.62 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; same psychology of desire arising from sight and thought, opposite evaluation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs declares love far more delightful than wine.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same comparison: love outdoes strong drink.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); near one-to-one on love surpassing wine, without the 'by sight alone' detail.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents love between spouses as a divine sign that brings peace and joy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural praises the joy of love; the Qur'an grounds that joy in God's design.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API (quoted to 'mercy'); a next-best match on love's joy, with no comparison to drink.

judaism.quote_or_event: Genesis says that Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him only a few days because of his love for her.
judaism.explanation: Love lets Jacob find delight simply in being near Rachel, even before marriage.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural, too, says love gives joy just by seeing, before anything is 'tasted'.
judaism.source: Genesis 29:20 (paraphrase; cf. JPS Tanakh on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; it shares love's joy through presence, not the wine comparison.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...a Sakyan girl — the envy of the countryside — glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, 'Hurry back, master.' Recollecting that, I don't enjoy leading the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: For Nanda, the memory of one glance is enough to unsettle his whole life as a monk.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says love intoxicates by sight alone; Nanda is intoxicated by the mere memory of a sight.
buddhism.source: Udana 3.2, Nanda Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; excerpt)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a strong fit on sight-born intoxication, which the sutta goes on to cure.

jainism.quote_or_event: “...thus she was seen by Rathanêmi, whose (peace of) mind became (thereby) disturbed...”
jainism.explanation: In the Uttaradhyayana, the monk Rathanemi happens to see Rajimati sheltering from the rain in a cave, and the sight alone throws his mind into turmoil.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says love acts through sight alone; this Jain story shows the same, as a warning.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; excerpt)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (excerpt); strong on sight alone stirring passion, but in a story about keeping monastic vows.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Narcissus falls in love simply by looking at a beautiful face in a pool, and cannot tear himself away from the sight.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's myth shows love born and fed entirely through the eyes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural, too, says love can intoxicate by sight alone.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked against a live text; the 'sight alone' element matches, but the myth is a cautionary tale about self-love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant argued that a judgment of beauty is a 'disinterested' delight: we take pleasure in the beautiful simply in contemplating it, without needing to possess or consume it.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, beauty pleases in the act of looking, unlike the merely agreeable, which pleases through consumption.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's contrast exactly: drink must be consumed, but beauty delights the one who only sees.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Kant's well-known doctrine, not checked against a live text; strong structural match, though Kant's disinterested beauty excludes desire, which the Kural's love does not.
